extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, agency counsel, and judges reviewing rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluate when an agency may properly invoke the APA’s good cause exception to bypass prepromulgation notice-and-comment by issuing an interim final rule (IFR), and what limits, review standards, and procedural safeguards should apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: APA good cause statutory grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA permits agencies to adopt a rule without notice-and-comment when the agency shows good cause that such procedures are "impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three statutory phrases are the baseline legal test agencies invoke; agencies must incorporate “the finding and a brief statement of reasons” per 5 U.S.C. §553(b)(B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Good cause grounded in an unforeseen emergency
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice-and-comment is "impracticable" when delay would prevent the agency from addressing an unforeseen emergency threatening life, health, safety, or national security.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have traditionally limited this ground to genuine emergencies (e.g., imminent threats) rather than mere desirability of faster policy change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good cause for uncontroversial or trivial rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Notice-and-comment is "unnecessary" when the rule is uncontroversial — no interested person would object — or so trivial that soliciting comments would not justify the cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies commonly use direct final rules for uncontroversial measures; invocation on this basis is relatively uncontroversial and not the Article’s focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good cause when notice would be contrary to the public interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The exception applies if giving notice would undermine the effectiveness of the rule (e.g., notice would trigger the very behavior the rule seeks to prevent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classic example: a rule restricting bank withdrawals to avert a bank run; notice would prompt the run and defeat the rule’s purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of justification on the agency
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies bear the burden of showing good cause and must include the finding and a brief statement of reasons in the rulemaking record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a procedural requirement under 5 U.S.C. §553(b)(B) intended to enable meaningful judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrow construction principle (traditional view)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have repeatedly said the good cause exception should be construed narrowly so it does not swallow the APA’s notice-and-comment requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although often stated, court application varies case-by-case; the Article argues for a softened application in appropriate cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost of delay as a factor
rubrics_metrics.description: Long lag times and regulatory delay are a legitimate consideration: the costs of delaying a beneficial rule may weigh in favor of invoking good cause/issuing an IFR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess delay costs (economic, health, regulatory effectiveness) against the foregone benefits of prepromulgation comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of IFR to reconcile speed and comment
rubrics_metrics.description: An interim final rule (IFR) lets a rule take effect immediately while inviting postpromulgation comments and possible amendment in a later "final final rule" (FFR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IFRs can solve the timing conundrum by providing immediate effect without forgoing eventual consideration of public input—but they also change the dynamic of the rulemaking process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Net social welfare test for IFR permissibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should permit expanded use of the good cause exception (and issuance of IFRs) when issuing an IFR and the ultimate FFR is "likely to best serve the public interest"—i.e., results in a net increase in social welfare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a balancing test weighing speed benefits against potential harms to rule quality; courts should ask whether the IFR+FFR pathway likely improves overall welfare relative to the status quo or to a NOPR route.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective-superiority requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An IFR should be justified only if there is evidence that the IFR is objectively superior to the regulatory status quo ante (not merely an agency value preference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should present objective evidence (data, analyses) showing the IFR is an improvement; mere value judgments or policy preferences are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficiency of pure value judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Value judgments alone are insufficient to justify issuance of an IFR under the expanded standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because value-laden preferences are common, courts should require an evidentiary showing that the IFR meaningfully improves outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of a permanent IFR
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies and courts should guard against IFRs becoming effectively permanent without adequate deliberation; the "problem of permanent IFRs" counsels limits on IFR use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural safeguards and active judicial review help prevent IFRs from becoming de facto final rules without meaningful consideration of comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: IFR as an imperfect substitute for a NOPR — logical outgrowth and NOPR-equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: When an IFR substitutes for a notice of proposed rulemaking (NOPR), courts should evaluate whether the IFR provided adequate notice and constitutes a logical outgrowth for the later FFR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Challenges may claim an IFR failed to include information required of a NOPR or that the FFR is not a logical outgrowth; such adequacy questions are judged under the same standards as NOPR adequacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: IFR’s effect on the content and composition of comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Issuing an IFR may alter who comments and the content of comments (e.g., more organized interest-group comments, fewer effective outsider comments), potentially reducing deliberative benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should consider whether the IFR will distort the comment process (chilling or channeling comments) in ways that undermine quality of the eventual FFR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding significant path dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should avoid issuing IFRs that create significant path dependence—mechanisms or expectations that lock in the IFR’s approach and make revising it harder even if comments warrant change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether issuance of the IFR will unduly bias the later decisionmaking process (confirmation bias, institutional inertia) and whether safeguards can limit path dependence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ameliorating confirmation bias via procedural safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Because adoption of an IFR can trigger confirmation bias, agencies and courts should rely on postpromulgation notice-and-comment plus 'hard look' judicial review to ensure agencies consider disconfirming evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly instructing agencies to address alternative hypotheses and disconfirming data in the FFR preamble and applying rigorous judicial review reduces bias risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailored standard of judicial review for good cause/IFR decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither simple de novo review nor blanket arbitrary-and-capricious deference is appropriate for all aspects of good-cause/IFR review; courts must evaluate legislative facts, predictions, and evidentiary showings with a calibrated approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts should demand evidentiary justification for agency predictions and legislative-fact inferences central to the good-cause determination, while acknowledging courts’ limits in resolving complex policy predictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that agencies justify factual predictions as 'most likely' resolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: When agencies rely on policy predictions or legislative facts to justify issuing an IFR, courts should require agencies to justify why their factual determinations and predictions are the most likely outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mitigates the danger of agencies asserting speculative benefits to justify bypassing notice-and-comment; agencies should supply supporting analysis and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation when statutory deadlines exist
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory deadlines may justify invoking the good cause exception only when compliance with notice-and-comment would make meeting the deadline virtually impossible or Congress clearly intended to permit bypassing notice-and-comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies cannot deliberately delay ("dawdle") and then invoke good cause on the eve of a deadline; courts scrutinize timing and feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere desire for speed not enough
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere desire to effectuate policy faster—without showing the IFR is objectively better or the delay would cause real harm—is ordinarily insufficient to justify bypassing notice-and-comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have rejected good cause claims grounded only in a wish to hasten policy implementation; agencies must show concrete necessity or benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy and meaningfulness of postpromulgation comment period
rubrics_metrics.description: When using an IFR, agencies must ensure the postpromulgation comment period is sufficiently long and meaningful to inform the FFR (e.g., allow time and information to test predictions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article suggests examples (e.g., an IFR effective in 60 days with a one-year comment period) and that preambles state that criteria may be broadened as comments warrant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts should guard against excessive deference (super-deference/thin rationality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the increased risk of bias when IFRs are used, courts should not apply excessive deference ("super deference" or "thin rationality") to agency choices but instead require robust justification and engagement with dissenting evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hard-look review is especially important where IFRs initiate the rulemaking process that culminates in an FFR.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive invalidity remains available
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if an IFR is procedurally justified under good cause, the IFR (or resulting FFR) can still be challenged as substantively invalid (beyond statutory authority or arbitrary and capricious).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural allowance of an IFR does not shield agencies from usual substantive review standards (e.g., Chevron, State Farm arbitrary-and-capricious review).

rubrics_metrics.name: Courts should weigh path-dependent harms versus benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: In deciding whether to tolerate broader use of IFRs, courts should weigh the benefits of immediate implementation against the risks that an IFR will distort the later rulemaking (altering comments, locking in biases, or producing a worse FFR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Article provides an explicit balancing framework: allow IFRs when likely welfare-improving, but restrict them when path-dependence, bias, or poor informational substitution make an IFR likely to reduce welfare.
